about: Rule catalog for yb-model. Each rule has a fixed base severity, a mechanism, a fix template and, where one exists, the yugabyte-db regress test that pins the behaviour. 'test' anchors are fixed strings that appear in src/postgres/src/test/regress/expected/<file>; scripts/check-rule-refs.py verifies them per release tag. kind: capability = decided by planner/storage code, independent of data; cost = depends on statistics and cost-model settings; stats = needs pg_stats; workload = needs pg_stat_statements; config = cluster settings; lint = DDL text only; plan = read from a replayed EXPLAIN. 'section': 'hygiene' marks rules about how the application uses the database; the report lists them separately for the application team. 'requires' lists settings a fix depends on; when rules/versions.json shows one absent on the customer's release, 'fix_if_unavailable' replaces 'fix'. No release numbers are written by hand: release facts come from versions.json (extracted from yugabyte-db) and observations.json (written by the planner oracle).

CAP001.title: Hash key not fully bound: index unusable for this pattern
CAP001.mechanism: A hash-sharded key is located by hashing every column of the hash group. A predicate that binds only part of the group, or binds it with a range, cannot compute the hash code, so the planner cannot use the index as an access path and falls back to a scan with a storage filter. With the cost model on, the planner may instead show an Index Scan with an Index Cond on the bound hash columns; it is still a full scan. Its probe checks this on the customer's release.
CAP001.fix: A hash group the pattern does not bind completely cannot locate rows by hash; the options are binding every hash column, or an index on the columns it binds.

test.anchor: EXPLAIN SELECT * from t4 where h1 = 1;
EXPLAIN SELECT * from t4 where h1 = 1 and h2 > 10;

CREATE TABLE ybm_p01 (h1 int NOT NULL, h2 int NOT NULL, r int NOT NULL, v text, PRIMARY KEY ((h1, h2) HASH, r ASC));
INSERT INTO ybm_p01 SELECT n % 50, n, n, repeat('x', 50) FROM generate_series(1, 20000) n;
ANALYZE ybm_p01;

CAP003.title: Only non-sargable predicates on this table
CAP003.mechanism: The pattern filters this table only with predicates no LSM index can seek on: inequality (!=, NOT IN), a leading-wildcard LIKE, a function on a column without a matching expression index, or a row comparison over hash keys. The predicate becomes a storage filter over a full scan.
CAP003.fix: Only non-seekable predicates reach the table; see the options.

CAP010.title: ORDER BY not served by the access path: explicit sort
CAP010.mechanism: Rows come back in index order only when every hash column is bound by equality and the ORDER BY columns follow the remaining range columns in key order, all in the key direction or all reversed. Otherwise the executor sorts every matching row before LIMIT can apply.
CAP010.fix: The access path does not deliver the requested order, so rows are sorted; see the options.

CAP011.title: IN-list on hash key with ORDER BY range column and LIMIT
CAP011.mechanism: Each IN value is a separate hash bucket, so no single index stream is ordered. Without merge scan streams the executor fetches every matching row from every bucket and sorts. With yb_max_merge_scan_streams above 0 the storage layer merges the ordered streams and LIMIT stops early.
CAP011.fix: Without merge scan streams every matching row of every IN value is fetched and sorted before LIMIT. yb_max_merge_scan_streams above 0 (per session or role, validated on the target release) lets LIMIT stop early; one query per key, or a range-sharded key, would also avoid the sort.

CAP011.fix_if_unavailable: This release has no merge scan streams, so every matching row of every IN value is fetched and sorted before LIMIT; one query per key (UNION ALL ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT), a range-sharded key, or an upgrade would avoid it.

CAP020.title: Secondary index does not cover the pattern: base-table fetch
CAP020.mechanism: An Index Only Scan needs every referenced column (projection, filter, ordering) in the index key or INCLUDE list. Otherwise each matching index row costs a distributed lookup into the base table, a network hop rather than a local page read.
CAP020.fix: The index lacks columns the query reads, so each row is fetched from the base table; see the options.

CAP021.title: Partial index predicate not implied by the query
CAP021.mechanism: The planner uses a partial index only when it can prove the query's WHERE implies the index's WHERE. A generic parameter or a missing predicate breaks the proof, so the index is ignored.
CAP021.fix: The query does not imply the index predicate, so the partial index cannot serve it; see the options.

CAP030.title: Partitioned table probed without the partition key: fan-out
CAP030.mechanism: Without a predicate on the partition key the planner cannot prune, so it probes every partition. Each probe is at least one distributed read, so latency grows with partition count even for a point lookup.
CAP030.fix: A query without the partition key probes every partition; the options are supplying the key in the query, or partitioning on what the queries bind.

CAP031.title: Join column on the inner side has no usable index
CAP031.mechanism: Batched nested loop joins push the outer keys into the inner index as an IN list. If no index on the inner table is bound by the join columns, the inner side is a full scan per batch or the planner picks a hash join that reads the whole inner table.
CAP031.fix: An index on the inner table's join column (as the full hash group or the leading range column) would let each outer row seek.

test.anchor: YB Batched Nested Loop Join

CAP040.title: OR across columns needs a bitmap scan
CAP040.mechanism: An OR over different columns cannot use a single index range. It needs a BitmapOr over several indexes, which only exists when bitmap scans are enabled; otherwise the table is scanned.
CAP040.fix: With yb_enable_bitmapscan on the target and an index on each OR arm, or as a UNION ALL of seekable queries, each arm would seek; confirm the setting there.

STA001.title: Nullable leading hash column holds many NULLs
STA001.mechanism: All NULLs hash to one code, so they land in one tablet. A tablet whose split key would reduce to that single hash code cannot be split, so it grows without bound. A unique index declared NULLS NOT DISTINCT admits at most one NULL key and is exempt.
STA001.fix: All NULL keys hash to one tablet; see the options.

STA004.title: Monotonic leading range key on a written table
STA004.mechanism: When values arrive in increasing order (a sequence, a creation timestamp), every insert lands in the last range tablet. That tablet is a write hotspot, and splitting only moves the hotspot to the new last tablet. In YSQL, pg_stats correlation measures agreement with the primary key order, not insert order, so the rule needs a sequence default, a time-typed or creation-named column, or (for a secondary index) correlation with a primary key that is itself insert-ordered. Measured writes raise its severity and confidence but never fire it alone.
STA004.fix: Insert-ordered keys concentrate inserts on one tablet; see the options.

WRK001.title: Measured read amplification
WRK001.mechanism: DocDB scanned many more rows than it returned for this statement, which is the signature of a scan doing an index's job or a storage filter discarding most rows.
WRK001.fix: Follow the access-path finding for this pattern; if none, inspect EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST).

WRK002.title: Many read RPCs per execution
WRK002.mechanism: Each execution makes many storage read requests, which points at partition fan-out, per-row base-table lookups from a non-covering index, or unbatched nested loops.
WRK002.fix: Follow the access-path finding for this pattern; confirm with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST).

WRK003.title: Index never scanned
WRK003.mechanism: idx_scan is 0 since statistics were last reset, yet every write to the table maintains the index as an extra participant.
WRK003.fix: An index no node scans costs writes; whether it is unused depends on idx_scan on every node and on jobs outside the capture window.

CFG001.title: Planner runs without the cost model or without statistics
CFG001.mechanism: With the YB cost model off, or with statistics unused, the planner picks index versus scan with heuristics that ignore table size and selectivity. Plans then change when the setting changes.
CFG001.fix: Run ANALYZE on every table and evaluate yb_enable_cbo=on (or yb_enable_base_scans_cost_model and yb_enable_optimizer_statistics on older releases) in staging.

test.anchor: yb_enable_base_scans_cost_model

CFG002.title: Default sharding is ASC here, and keys rely on the default
CFG002.mechanism: In a colocated database, a tablegroup, or with yb_use_hash_splitting_by_default off, an unannotated first key column is range-sharded, not hashed. Keys written assuming HASH get range semantics.
CFG002.fix: Keys whose lead column carries no explicit HASH, ASC or DESC take the default of the server and tool that create them, so the same DDL can shard differently elsewhere.

CFG003.title: DocDB statement statistics not available
CFG003.mechanism: pg_stat_statements has no docdb_* values, so read amplification and RPC counts per statement cannot be measured.

SPL001.title: Large relation still on one tablet
SPL001.mechanism: The relation (table or index) holds many rows but has one tablet, so one tserver leads every write to it until auto-split catches up, and auto-split of a hot tablet is itself disruptive. Indexes never inherit the table's split.
SPL001.fix: A relation created or rebuilt with SPLIT INTO <n> TABLETS, sized from its expected mature size and the node count, starts with its load spread; existing ones grow tablets only if auto-split is enabled, which is worth confirming.

PRT001.title: Partition runway running out
PRT001.mechanism: Inserts whose partition key falls past the last RANGE partition fail with 'no partition of relation found' when there is no DEFAULT partition. Nothing in the schema creates partitions ahead of time.
PRT001.fix: Inserts past the last partition fail unless a job creates partitions well ahead of need; confirm that job exists and covers the next periods. Retention, if any, is the same job's concern, and a DEFAULT partition is a safety net that later needs cleanup.

STA006.title: Columns never set in the sampled rows
STA006.mechanism: A column with no non-NULL value in the sampled rows carries no data but still costs schema surface, ORM mapping and row width in replication and CDC. Columns an index references, event timestamps that stay NULL until the event happens, and columns that hold some data are left out.
STA006.fix: Ask the application owners whether these columns are still written. Dropping a column also drops every index whose key, INCLUDE list or predicate references it; the columns listed are referenced by none.

STA007.title: Sentinel value in place of real data
STA007.mechanism: A large share of rows hold a placeholder such as 0001-01-01, so the column no longer means what its name says and range predicates on it misbehave.
STA007.fix: Store NULL or the real value; backfill where possible.

STA008.title: Index on a boolean column
STA008.mechanism: A boolean has at most two key values, so a hash index on it has two hash codes (two hot tablets at most) and no selectivity worth an index.
STA008.fix: A boolean key has at most two values, so each is one large range on one tablet; see the options.

WRK005.title: Hot lookup that always returns no rows
WRK005.mechanism: Every call pays a distributed read for an empty answer.
WRK005.fix: Confirm with the application why the lookup misses; cache the negative result or skip the call.

WRK006.title: Planning time is a large share of statement time
WRK006.mechanism: Statements are re-planned on most executions, so short OLTP lookups spend a large share of their time in the planner.
WRK006.fix: Enable protocol-level prepared statements with plan caching in the driver or ORM.

CFG004.title: Primary key sharding not visible in the dump
CFG004.mechanism: Without --include-yb-metadata the dump omits HASH/ASC annotations and tablet splits, so the actual sharding of every unannotated primary key is inferred from defaults rather than observed.
CFG004.fix: A dump taken with ysql_dump --schema-only --include-yb-metadata would show the sharding as created; keys with no explicit HASH, ASC or DESC take the default of whatever creates them.

CFG005.title: Tables without statistics
CFG005.mechanism: Tables with no pg_stats rows have never been analyzed, so the cost model plans them with defaults.
CFG005.fix: ANALYZE them and confirm auto-analyze is enabled.

CAP050.title: Primary key does not serve the table's lookups
CAP050.mechanism: Every ranked read goes through the same non-covering secondary index and then fetches each row from the base table by its primary key: two distributed reads per row where a primary key led by the lookup column would need one.
CAP050.fix: Lookups by another column fetch every row from the base table; see the options.

WRK007.title: Lookup returns many rows per call
WRK007.mechanism: Each call reads and ships thousands of rows. When the measured rows per call far exceed what the column's cardinality predicts, calls concentrate on the heaviest values.
WRK007.fix: Confirm the application needs every row (paginate or narrow the projection); for heavy values consider a summary table or caching.

WRK008.title: Full-table aggregate in the workload
WRK008.mechanism: COUNT(*) or GROUP BY without a filter reads every row of a large table on every call, competing with OLTP traffic.
WRK008.fix: For monitoring counts use pg_class.reltuples or an approximate count; for analytics, run against a read replica or with follower reads.

WRK009.title: UPDATE or DELETE that mostly matches nothing
WRK009.mechanism: Most calls find no row to change, yet each still pays a distributed read and, for UPDATE, a write-intent check.
WRK009.fix: Confirm with the application why most calls match nothing; check existence once or batch the writes.

WRK010.title: UPDATE rewrites key or creation-time columns
WRK010.mechanism: The SET list includes columns the WHERE clause already pins, or creation-time columns, which is the signature of an ORM writing every column. It adds write cost and can clobber values (for example created_at).
WRK010.fix: Configure the ORM to write changed columns only (partial updates).

CAP051.title: Primary key unused beside a unique secondary
CAP051.mechanism: Every ranked read goes through a unique secondary index and then fetches the row by primary key: two distributed reads where one would do if the unique key were the primary key.
CAP051.fix: Reads go through the unique index and then fetch the row; see the options.

test.anchor: -- test index only scan with non-target column refs in qual (github issue #9176)

options.label: Make the unique key the primary key, keep the old key unique (a table swap)
options.when: every hot read goes through the unique key
options.tradeoff: a copy of the table and a swap; foreign keys must move
options.check_first: every pattern and foreign key that uses the current primary key

options.label: Cover the reads with INCLUDE on the unique index
options.when: the read columns are few and small
options.tradeoff: a larger index
options.check_first: column sizes

options.label: Accept the fetch
options.when: the reads are not hot
options.tradeoff: one base-table read per row
options.check_first: the pattern weights

CAP012.title: Ordered index walk with a filter until LIMIT
CAP012.mechanism: No index can seek on the filter, but a range-led index matches ORDER BY, so the planner reads it in order and filters each row until LIMIT rows match. When matches are rare, that is most of the index.
CAP012.fix: An index with the filter columns first and the ORDER BY columns after them would seek and read only the LIMIT rows.

CAP060.title: ON CONFLICT target has no matching unique index
CAP060.mechanism: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) needs a unique index or constraint whose key columns are exactly cols (in any order; a partial one only when the statement repeats its predicate in ON CONFLICT (cols) WHERE ...). ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT name needs a primary key or unique constraint of that name; a unique index that backs no constraint cannot be named. Without one the statement fails with 'there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification' on every execution, so the idempotent write it was meant to provide never happens.
CAP060.fix: Without a unique index on exactly the conflict columns the statement fails; see the options.

options.when: the columns must be unique together

options.check_first: that the columns are NOT NULL and have no duplicates today

options.label: Change the statement's target to an existing unique key
options.when: an existing unique index already decides conflicts
options.tradeoff: an application change
options.check_first: that the existing key gives the intended conflict behaviour

options.label: Leave it as it is
options.when: the cost is acceptable for how the application uses this object, or another finding's change settles it
options.tradeoff: the defect stays
options.check_first: how the workload will grow

PLN005.title: Replayed pattern fails on the release
PLN005.mechanism: The pattern was planned on the customer's release with the customer's schema and the planner rejected it. The application will get the same error.
PLN005.fix: Read the error with the pattern; fix the statement or the schema object it depends on.

test.anchor: ERROR:  there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification

CAP013.title: Keyset cursor is a row comparison only: rechecked, not sought
CAP013.mechanism: A cursor written as (a, b) < ($1, $2) appears in the plan as an Index Cond, but DocDB does not turn a row comparison into a seek bound: it scans from the start of the key prefix and the row comparison removes the rows before the cursor on recheck, after their base-table rows are fetched. Page n reads every row of pages 1..n. A plain bound on the first column (a <= $1) is pushed down as a seek. Its probe checks this on the customer's release.
CAP013.fix: DocDB seeks on a plain bound on the cursor's first column, not on the row comparison, which is only rechecked.

CAP014.title: Key column bound after an unbound one: a seek per value of the gap
CAP014.mechanism: The pattern binds the key's hash columns and leading range columns, leaves one or more range columns unbound (or only filtered, as with != or LIKE), and binds a later key column. DocDB cannot seek on the later column directly: it seeks under every distinct value of the gap columns within the bound prefix (a skip scan), so rows scanned stay close to rows returned while seeks grow with the number of distinct gap values. Plans show an Index Scan with the later column in its Index Cond; only seek counts (EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, DIST, DEBUG)) or timing show the cost. Its probe checks this on the customer's release. The regress test pins the plan shape (a later key column in the Index Cond with an earlier one unbound); the probe measures the seeks.

test.anchor: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT g, max(a) FROM t_23709 WHERE t <= '2024-09-30 00:00:00 +0000' GROUP BY g;

CAP014.fix: The read costs a seek per distinct value of the skipped key columns, not per row returned; see the options.

options.label: Put the bound columns before the skipped ones in the primary key (a table swap)
options.when: the reads that skip are hot and no hot read binds the skipped columns without the moved one
options.tradeoff: a copy of the table and a swap; reads that bind the skipped columns but not the moved one get the gap instead
options.check_first: every pattern that reads through the primary key, and the foreign keys that reference the table

options.label: Rebuild the index with the bound columns before the skipped ones
options.when: the reads that skip are hot and no hot read binds the skipped columns without the moved one
options.tradeoff: a rebuild; reads that bind the skipped columns but not the moved one get the gap instead
options.check_first: every pattern that reads through the index

options.label: Add an index that leads with the bound columns
options.when: both orders are read often
options.tradeoff: another copy of the key written on every insert and key update; reads that need other columns fetch them from the base table unless it covers them
options.check_first: the table's write rate and the columns the reads return

options.label: Accept the seeks
options.when: the skipped columns have few values under the bound prefix
options.tradeoff: a seek per distinct value of the skipped columns on every such read
options.check_first: the distinct counts of the skipped columns (pg_stats)

MEAS001.title: Unexplained, measured: the read does more work than the rows it returns
MEAS001.mechanism: The measured pass ran the read on a small sample generated from the bundle's statistics (none of the customer's data; only the constants the statements bind), with the plan chosen under the full-scale statistics when the bundle has them, and counted DocDB seeks and rows scanned per row returned. The counts crossed a threshold and no finding on the pattern explains them. It is a lead for a closer look, not a diagnosis: the sample's shape is an estimate, and the plan on the customer's cluster may differ.
MEAS001.fix: No rule covers this measurement: it is a lead for a closer look, and once explained it becomes a rule or a pitfalls.md entry.
